query: Mg-containing lightweight high-entropy alloys have reported densities of 1.46–6 g/cm3 and commonly contain solid solutions together with intermetallic compounds. Earlier induction-melted Al–Mg-rich alloys established this structural complexity but did not resolve subsequent transformation pathways. Compositionally graded MgAlCuZnGd alloys showed region-dependent compression and corrosion performance, while studies of AlMgₓTiSnZn alloys associated Mg content with phase stability and multiple functional properties. Most prior work emphasized hardness and room-temperature compression, leaving corrosion, high-temperature oxidation, and evolution from metastable states comparatively underexplored. Within the design constraint of density below 6 g/cm3 and the tendency for constituent-property differences to promote stable intermetallic compounds, what single testable mechanistic hypothesis could explain how a non-equilibrium Mg-containing lightweight high-entropy alloy evolves and why that evolution changes its corrosion and high-temperature oxidation behavior? Specify an unnamed controlled comparison, predictions relative to the initial baseline, boundary conditions, supporting prior observations, and an outcome that would falsify the hypothesis.

generation.hypothesis: The evolution of non-equilibrium Mg-containing lightweight high-entropy alloys under high-temperature oxidation and corrosion conditions is driven by the transformation of metastable phases into stable intermetallic compounds, which in turn alters the alloy's corrosion and high-temperature oxidation behavior.
generation.mechanism: Transformation of metastable phases into stable intermetallic compounds through diffusion and precipitation processes
generation.predicted_outcome: Improved corrosion resistance and reduced high-temperature oxidation rates due to the formation of stable intermetallic compounds
generation.baseline: Initial non-equilibrium state with metastable phases
generation.uncertainty: The exact transformation pathways and the role of constituent-property differences in promoting stable intermetallic compounds are not well understood

falsification_experiment.design: In situ transmission electron microscopy (TEM) or X-ray diffraction (XRD) to monitor phase transformations and corrosion processes in real-time
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: If no significant transformation of metastable phases into stable intermetallic compounds is observed, and no corresponding change in corrosion and high-temperature oxidation behavior is detected, the hypothesis is falsified

decision.trend: Research has been focused on understanding the properties and behavior of high-entropy alloys, including their mechanical properties, corrosion resistance, and high-temperature oxidation behavior. Earlier studies have explored the effects of composition, processing, and microstructure on these properties. However, the evolution of non-equilibrium Mg-containing lightweight high-entropy alloys and their transformation pathways remain poorly understood.
decision.unsolved: The lack of understanding of the transformation pathways and evolution from metastable states in Mg-containing lightweight high-entropy alloys, particularly in relation to their corrosion and high-temperature oxidation behavior.
decision.lever: in situ high-temperature X-ray diffraction (HTXRD) and transmission electron microscopy (TEM)
decision.why: To investigate the phase transformations and microstructural evolution of Mg-containing lightweight high-entropy alloys during high-temperature oxidation and corrosion, and to understand the underlying mechanisms driving their mechanical properties and corrosion resistance.
